linkages: individuals are grouped into households of one or two adults: two adults count as one household if they live together and are married or in a registered partnership, or have at least one common child registered in the Civil Registration System, or are of opposite sex with an age difference of 15 years or less, not closely related, and live in a household with no other adults
an individual's household changes if he or she marries or divorces, so household panels break on family formation and dissolution
income and wealth are linked through the household budget constraint to impute expenditure
US households in the 2016 SCF are linked to the Danish estimates by interpolating the percentile of liquid wealth of the median household in each decile on the Danish MPX-by-liquid-wealth schedule

sample.universe: the entire Danish population of households (one or two adults) in the registers 2003-2015; the estimation universe is households headed by an individual aged 30-55 in 2008
sample.unit_of_observation: household-year (with parameters estimated per subpopulation from 3-, 4- and 5-year growth spells)
selection_rules: define a household as one or two adults (married/registered partners, parents of a common child, or an opposite-sex couple with an age difference of 15 years or less living with no other adults)
limit the sample to households headed by an individual between the ages of 30 and 55 in 2008
remove business owners and households receiving more than a trivial amount of income from business ventures
remove households in the top and bottom 1 percent of the income distribution
exclude households in years in which they are involved in a housing transaction, which requires no housing transaction over a five-year window
require households to survive (have reliable data) for at least five consecutive years
discard both income and expenditure data for household-years with negative imputed expenditure (about 3 percent of households)
for households holding significant equity investments, assume they hold a diversified index of stocks when imputing capital gains
sample.n_observations: 8,081,348 household-year observations (estimation sample); 18,050,340 in the age 30-55 population

construction_notes: expenditure is imputed from the household budget constraint C_t = Y_t - P_t - dNW_t, where P_t is contributions to privately administered pension schemes and dNW_t is the change in (nonpension, nonhousing) net worth measured at the end of years t and t-1
housing wealth is excluded from net worth for the imputation only; the measure of net wealth used where wealth itself is of interest (e.g. Table 2) includes housing
imputed expenditure captures both durable and nondurable expenditure, hence the label Marginal Propensity to eXpend (MPX) rather than MPC
income is after-tax and transfer total household labour income; baseline results use total household labour income, with head-of-household income as a robustness check (online Appendix L)

income and expenditure are normalised by average household income over the observed period and replaced by the residual of a regression on dummies for age, year, highest level of education, marital status, homeowner status and number of children, plus interactions of age with education, marital status and homeowner status
the change in these residuals is taken to be the unexpected income (expenditure) change from one year to the next
liquid wealth is defined as the mean bank deposit holding over the entire sample period; quintile bounds are rounded to the nearest $1,000
net wealth includes housing and debts; URE and NNP are divided by mean sample expenditure when plotted
URE and NNP can only be calculated for 2009-2015 because mortgage information is insufficiently detailed in earlier years
all monetary values are reported in 2015 US dollars
the model is estimated in levels rather than logs so that the parameters are marginal propensities; a log specification is reported in online Appendix L
the estimator uses 96 moments: 8 consecutive five-year periods, each with three 3-year, two 4-year and one 5-year growth periods, each contributing a variance and a covariance moment

definition.value: a proportional change in the income of all households in the economy; the paper's illustrative size is a 1 percent increase. In equation (7) it enters as dY/Y multiplied by the sufficient statistic M.

key_assumptions.assumption: Idiosyncratic income is the sum of a permanent component that follows a martingale (random walk) with independent increments and a transitory component that has decayed to zero within two years
key_assumptions.supported_by: follows Carroll and Samwick (1997); online Appendixes E, J and K explore transitory persistence, heterogeneous income profile models and time-varying risk models

key_assumptions.assumption: Consumption responds to a permanent income shock as a random walk proportional to the shock (parameter phi), and its response to a transitory shock follows a generic path g(t) that has fallen to zero two years after the news of the shock
key_assumptions.supported_by: Gelman (2021) and Fagereng, Holm, and Natvik (2021) show the response has (almost entirely) decayed two years after the shock; online Appendix I bounds the residual bias
